analysis.one_liner: Requires insurers to disclose full coverage terms and lets treating doctors decide medically necessary care.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in a House Commerce subcommittee from November 1995 until the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required health insurers to tell enrollees exactly what their plans cover — and what they exclude — every year. It would have taken the decision about what care is "medically necessary" away from insurance company reviewers and given it to the doctors actually treating the patient, and required insurers to pay for covered services those doctors order. It also would have banned insurers from paying or penalizing doctors based on how much care they withhold, and barred insurers from writing contracts that shield them from liability.
analysis.who_benefits: People enrolled in health insurance and HMO plans. They would get plain, annual written disclosure of covered and excluded services, copays, deductibles, and — notably — what share of their premium actually pays for care versus administration. Patients would no longer have coverage decisions made by insurer reviewers with no involvement in their care: their treating doctor's judgment of medical necessity would bind the insurer, and insurers could not offer doctors bonuses or threaten their plan participation for limiting tests and treatments. Insurers that violated the rules would face civil money penalties [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Under a health plan, only a licensed practitioner directly involved in the patient's care could decide what treatment is medically necessary and appropriate — not an insurer's utilization reviewer — and the insurer would have to pay for any covered service so determined.

Insurers would have to give every enrollee annual written notice of the plan's terms, including covered and excluded services, copayments, deductibles, premiums, utilization review requirements, usual and customary costs, and the percentage of premiums spent on practitioners' care versus administration and other costs.

The Secretary of Health and Human Services would write rules barring insurers from offering doctors monetary rewards, penalties, or inducements — or conditioning their continued participation in the plan — based on their decisions to limit appropriate tests, services, or treatments.

Insurers could no longer include hold-harmless clauses shielding themselves from liability in plan contracts, and violations of the act would carry civil money penalties set by HHS. States could not set standards weaker than the federal ones.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and HMOs. They would bear the cost of annual detailed disclosures to every enrollee, would lose the use of financial incentives that reward doctors for limiting care — a common managed-care cost-control tool — and would have to pay for treating doctors' medical-necessity determinations, with civil money penalties for violations. Some of those costs could be passed on in premiums, and insurers would lose a mechanism for holding down utilization.

drawbacks.text: Requiring insurers to pay for any service a treating practitioner deems medically necessary, with no independent cost-review step, could push up premiums and encourage overtreatment — the concern managed-care utilization review was designed to address.

The annual disclosure mandate — a copy of the contract plus satisfaction statistics, lists of usual and customary costs, credentialing standards, and premium-spending breakdowns for every enrollee — would impose significant administrative and paperwork costs on insurers, some of which would likely be passed on in premiums.

The civil money penalty amount is left entirely to the discretion of the Secretary of Health and Human Services, so the deterrent's strength would depend on how aggressively a given administration set and enforced it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade-off is real but modest by design: the bill targets the most criticized practices of 1990s managed care — opaque coverage terms and secret incentives to deny care — while leaving the private insurance system intact. Giving treating doctors the final word on medical necessity raises legitimate cost-control concerns, and the paperwork burden on insurers is genuine. But the bill keeps a check in place by limiting the guarantee to services the plan already covers, and it adds penalties and a state floor rather than a new entitlement. On balance the benefits for enrollees outweigh the compliance costs, though the insurer-pays framing means some of the cost would surface in premiums.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Commerce Committee and then to its Health and Environment subcommittee, which never acted on it before the Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Rep. Jerrold Nadler introduced the Health Care Consumer Protection Act of 1995 on November 9, 1995, joined by four original cosponsors — Reps. Dellums, Engel, McKinney, and Collins of Michigan.
The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on Commerce, and on November 20, 1995, to that committee's Subcommittee on Health and Environment.

Eight House Democrats cosponsored the bill in total. No further action — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — was ever taken, and the bill died when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and HMOs came out ahead: they never had to accept the disclosure requirements, the ban on denial-based incentives to doctors, or treating-doctor control of medical-necessity decisions.

sides.party_line_note: All nine sponsors were Democrats and the Republican-run Commerce Committee never acted on the bill, but no vote was ever recorded, so the partisan split can only be inferred.

industries.note: The bill would force annual detailed disclosure of coverage terms and premium spending, ban the financial incentives insurers used to reward doctors for limiting care, replace insurer reviewers with treating doctors on medical-necessity decisions, and expose insurers to civil money penalties and liability by banning hold-harmless clauses. Insurers lose a set of managed-care cost-control tools and gain compliance costs they could partly pass on in premiums.
